factProposals.value: Process analysis takes a process event log: a process name and one row per step with caseId, activity, actor, startedAt and endedAt (ISO 8601 with a time zone). Until a Microsoft 365 / Google Workspace connector exists it is supplied as JSON.

A detailed report (JSON and readable text): numbered findings for bottlenecks, duplicated work and automation candidates, each with an explanation, the numbers and example cases, plus the method used and what the report cannot tell you.
Only the process analyst and operations manager roles may run an analysis or read a saved one; anyone else is refused and the refusal is logged.

Incomplete or malformed data (missing fields, timestamps without a time zone, steps ending before they start, fewer than 3 complete cases) stops the analysis; the user gets a notice listing each problem by field, row and case. An interrupted or timed-out analysis saves nothing and can be re-run.
Automation candidates are steps in at least 30% of cases that usually take 15 minutes or less with a consistent duration; they are flagged as candidates only, with no savings estimate.
Every analysis activity (request, start, completion, missing data, refusal, interruption, replay) is written to the hash-chained audit log with the requesting user's id and a timestamp.

decisions.statement: Refuse to analyse incomplete data and list what is missing, rather than analysing the complete rows and flagging the rest.
decisions.rationale: A report built on gaps could point at the wrong bottleneck. Chosen by the student before building.

decisions.statement: Allow the process analyst and operations manager roles to run analyses.
decisions.rationale: They are the roles in the plan that own process analysis and orchestration. Chosen by the student before building.

decisions.statement: Find inefficiencies with explicit, named rules and thresholds (2x typical or 25% of case time for bottlenecks; 30% frequency, 15 minutes or less and consistent duration for automation; at least 3 observations), reported in every report.
decisions.rationale: Every finding must be explainable to the person reading it.

decisions.statement: Run the process analyst as a real agent under the STORY-001 orchestrator, returning refused requests and missing data as results rather than agent failures.
decisions.rationale: Throwing them would take a healthy agent out of rotation over a bad request.

decisions.statement: Treat steps that start at the same instant as concurrent: each gets the same wait, and results (and finding order) do not depend on the order of rows in the input or the time zone timestamps are written in.
decisions.rationale: Found by a randomised stress test: the row listed first used to take the whole wait, so the same data could blame a different step for a bottleneck.

decisions.statement: Add a third kind of agent failure, TaskFailedError ("this task failed, the agent is fine"): the orchestrator fails the task at once, keeps the agent in rotation and marks the operation failed so it re-runs. The process analyst raises it for an interrupted analysis.
decisions.rationale: Found in code review: an interrupted analysis came back as normal output, so the orchestrator saved the operation as completed and replayed "interrupted" for ever; blaming the agent instead would have taken the only process analyst out of rotation.

decisions.statement: Give the analysis service a shorter time limit than the orchestrator (demo: 60 s vs 90 s).
decisions.rationale: Then a slow analysis stops itself and reports interrupted; if the orchestrator limit fired first it would treat the agent as failed and take it out of rotation for its cooldown.

limitations.statement: There is no login: the user id and role are whatever the caller states. The permission check is real; identity is not verified.
Durations are clock time, so waits include nights and weekends; there is no working-hours calendar.
Bottlenecks are judged relative to the process's own typical step and wait, so in a process of very short steps a moderately long step can be flagged.
Validation of the input runs in one go and cannot be interrupted; only the analysis itself is subject to the time limit.
The only data analysed so far is synthetic demo data; no real organisation's process has been analysed.

The service-shorter-than-orchestrator time limit is a wiring rule documented in code, not enforced: a deployment that sets them the other way round would take the process analyst out of rotation on a slow analysis.
